Leonardo, it is Claire Whitmore. I got your two pages and I read them on the train, which is the best review I can give you. Two things before Thursday. First, the answer is clear and I could follow it from the first line to the last, so whatever you changed since January, keep doing that. Second, and I want to be direct about it. The third paragraph does not address the question I asked. It is accurate. It is also about the two thousand and twenty-one file, and I did not ask about the two thousand and twenty-one file. If the board reads that paragraph, they will think we are defending something. Cut it, or move it to an annex. One more thing, and this is not a criticism. You use the word significant four times on page one. Pick a different word three times, or pick a number. A number is never vague. I will be on the call at nine, and I will have the chairman with me, which I know you enjoy.

I have marked this examination for eleven years, and I want to tell you the one thing that separates the candidates who pass comfortably from the ones who fail by two marks. It is not vocabulary. The ones who fail by two marks read the question last. They read the passage carefully, from the first word, the way you would read a contract, and then they meet the question and they have to go back. That is four minutes gone, on a paper where you have seventy-five. So read the question first. Then skim the passage for the shape of it, thirty seconds, no more, and only then go looking for the answer. And when you go looking, remember what the paper is doing to you. The correct option almost never uses the words of the passage. It paraphrases them. So a candidate who is hunting for matching words is being led, on purpose, to the wrong answer. Two more things. If a question asks what the writer implies, the answer is not written down anywhere, and reading harder will not find it. And in the written part, nobody is counting your ideas. The examiner is asking whether your second sentence follows your first. One clear idea, defended, beats three ideas mentioned.

In my view, the rules are too complex for a foreign investor to navigate alone. This is supported by the fact that three separate authorities can review the same payment. One could argue that professional advice already solves the problem. However, it should be noted that the cost of that advice falls on the smallest investors. In conclusion, the evidence suggests that simplification would open the market rather than close it.
